queue.tree_name: The Black Locust of the Ciutadella
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.3 metres round on a tree only 12 metres tall, stout where black locusts are usually thin. It stands in the parterre between the Passeig de Joaquim Renart and the Cascada.
queue.story: A trunk of 4.3 metres on a tree only 12 metres tall makes this the stoutest black locust in Barcelona and the only one the city has ever put on its register. Black locusts usually run up thin and fast and then fall over. This one went sideways and stayed, and it grows in the parterre between the Passeig de Joaquim Renart and the Cascada, the monumental fountain a young Gaudi worked on as a student assistant. How old it is nobody has established. The register's age column holds the words '100 anys' where a planting year should be, which is somebody's estimate written into the wrong box rather than a date anyone has checked, and the tree was only catalogued in 2024. queue.tree_name: The Mexican Oak of the Ciutadella
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, leathery and plain edged with none of an oak's lobes, and by the leaning stem that throws an 11 metre crown sideways, low enough to put a hand on. It stands on the sand near the Ciutadella bandstand.
queue.story: An oak with no lobes in its leaves, and the only one of its kind alive in Catalonia. Quercus polymorpha grows wild from Texas down through Mexico into Guatemala and Honduras, keeping leathery, plain-edged leaves for most of the year, and almost nobody in Europe plants it. Barcelona's single specimen has been leaning out over the sand of Parc de la Ciutadella since about 1887, the year the park was being rebuilt for the Universal Exposition that opened next door the following spring.
